source.note: The source is this repository's own Python implementation, not a second checkout. Cadenza is being rewritten in place (cadenza#8): `src/cadenza/` and `tests/` are the specification until a later PR retires them, so every inventory here is collected from the working tree at the recorded revision.

suite_baseline.reconciliation: `PYTHONPATH=src PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python3 -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider` at a5672f8 on CPython 3.12.3: 330 passed. No module is skipped at collection time, so collected == the sum of the eight per-file inventories with nothing left over. See parity/source-inventory.manifest.json.

file.note: 9 test functions, 97 collected node ids. Five of the nine are parametrized over the modules the walk finds: four over all 20 Python modules and one over the 7 under `cadenza.domain`, which is 87 of the 97 by itself.

systematic_mappings.from: `@pytest.mark.parametrize("path", MODULES, ids=module_name)`, over the 20 Python modules `PACKAGE_ROOT.rglob("*.py")` finds
systematic_mappings.to: `parametrize(name, PER_MODULE, ...)` over the 18 TypeScript modules the walk over `src/` finds, with the repo-relative path as the id
systematic_mappings.why: This is the whole of why cadenza#8 re-points this file instead of transcribing it. The two module sets are not the same set with different spellings: 12 Python modules have a TypeScript counterpart, 8 are `__init__.py` package initialisers or `__about__.py` and have none, and 6 TypeScript modules exist that Python never had (`canonical-json`, `frozen`, and the four `python-*` standard-library ports, D-0018). So each of the four per-module functions contributes 12 `adapted` entries and 8 `waived` ones, and the 6 modules with no source case are declared `target_only_tests` rather than left unaccounted.
systematic_mappings.affects: 80 of the 97 cases: the four functions parametrized over all 20 modules

systematic_mappings.why: The id has to name the thing the case is about, and in this tree that is a file rather than a dotted module name. Paths are spelled with forward slashes on every platform, and the walk sorts them, so the ids are byte-stable across the ubuntu, macos and windows cells rather than depending on `readdirSync` order or the platform separator.

systematic_mappings.from: `imported_modules(path)`, an `ast.walk` collecting `ast.Import` and `ast.ImportFrom` with relative levels resolved
systematic_mappings.to: `importsIn(source, from)`, a `ts.createSourceFile` walk collecting import declarations, `export ... from` re-exports, `import(...)` calls, `require(...)` calls, `import x = require(...)`, `import("...").X` type nodes, and string-named `declare module "..."` augmentations, with relative specifiers resolved by path arithmetic
systematic_mappings.why: The source's docstring states the property that matters -- an import nested in a function or under `TYPE_CHECKING` is still an import, and importing the tree would not see either -- and TypeScript has strictly more routes with that property. A re-export has no Python counterpart at all and is how a layer leaks through a barrel, so the sweep covers it. A module augmentation has none either, and is the same kind of thing: `declare module "../application/compose.js" { ... }` inside an external module is resolved by the compiler exactly as an import is, and merges declarations into the module it names, so it is recorded rather than read as a namespace. Resolution is path arithmetic rather than a filesystem lookup, because the detector's own cases name modules that do not exist; `tsc` is what checks a specifier resolves, and this only has to agree about which file it resolves to.
systematic_mappings.affects: the 7 detector cases and all 87 per-module cases

systematic_mappings.to: `DOMAIN_ALLOWED_BUILTINS`, an allowlist naming both the module and the bindings it may contribute: `node:crypto` for `createHash`, `node:os` for `homedir`, `node:net` for `isIP`
systematic_mappings.why: A denylist is the wrong shape here for a reason specific to Node rather than to taste. `node:net` IS the socket module the source's denylist names first, and `isIP` is a pure predicate that happens to live in it, so a denylist either forbids `node:net` and fails on `src/domain/python-urlsplit.ts` today, or admits it and admits `createConnection` with it. Naming the bindings is what separates the two. The allowlist also fails closed, which the denylist does not: a `node:` module nobody thought of is a violation rather than an omission, and a namespace or default import of an allowed module is refused because neither can be checked binding by binding. Measured: a planted `import * as os from "node:os"` turns the case red, and so does `createConnection`.
systematic_mappings.affects: the 7 cases of 'the domain performs no I/O'

systematic_mappings.from: `FORBIDDEN_BY_LAYER`, a denylist naming the layers each layer may not import
systematic_mappings.to: `ALLOWED_BY_LAYER`, an allowlist naming the layers each layer may import, plus `UNLAYERED_MODULES` naming the one module that belongs to no layer and `ALLOWED_FOR_UNLAYERED` naming what that module may reach
systematic_mappings.why: The source's shape answers "no" for anything it was not told about, and the port has something the source does not: `src/index.ts`, a public barrel in no layer that re-exports across all of them. Under a denylist a domain module importing `../index.js` matched no forbidden prefix and passed, reaching `src/application` through the re-export; a directory added later would have been the same story. Raised at review of this belt and inverted. The allowlist also makes belonging to no layer fail rather than exempt: a new top-level module under `src/` is an offender until it is classified. And being allowed to have no layer changes which table answers the question rather than whether it is asked: the barrel is checked against the four layer roots, so `export { absolute } from "../test/support.js"` -- a re-export reaching out of the package, which no other case reads because `unapprovedExternalsIn` considers bare specifiers only -- is an offender. Measured: `../index.js` from `src/domain` and from `src/ports`, and a new `src/toplevel.ts`, each turn the expected case red.
systematic_mappings.affects: the 20 cases of 'each layer imports only inward'

systematic_mappings.to: the normalised package name of a bare specifier, and the unscoped half of a scoped one, matched against `{"claude-org-runtime", "interlock"}`
systematic_mappings.why: The source's two spellings are Python module names, and the same two dependencies would arrive here written differently: `claude_org_runtime` becomes `claude-org-runtime` on a registry, and either could be scoped as `@suisya-systems/interlock`. Lower-casing and folding `_` to `-`, then checking the unscoped half as well, covers all of those without enumerating them. Measured: `@suisya-systems/interlock` and `claude-org-runtime/control-plane.js` both turn the case red.
systematic_mappings.affects: the 20 cases of 'no module imports interlock'

target_only_tests.why: Thirty-five, in five groups. Thirty are the six TypeScript modules that have no Python counterpart -- `canonical-json`, `frozen` and the four `python-*` standard-library ports (D-0018) -- appearing in the five per-module functions; they are boundary cases with no source case because the modules themselves were created by the port. One is the detector's `require(...)` and `import x = require(...)` routes: `tsc` refuses both in an ESM module under D-0003, so no source case and no real module exercises them, and machinery nothing asserts is untested surface -- the rule `test/testkit/testkit.contract.test.ts` already records. The handling stays because the sweep should not depend on the module setting staying what it is today. Two are `src/application`'s no-I/O cases: design section 8 marks `application/` `(no I/O)` in the same code block that marks `domain/`, and the source parametrises its case over the domain alone -- so under D-0001's oracle order the document's wider claim is the one enforced, and the two extra cases translate no source case because none was written. The last is the global-I/O sweep, a surface the port created rather than inherited: reaching the network in Python means importing something, which is why a denylist over modules was a complete answer there, while Node hands `fetch` to every module for free and `console` writes to a stream nobody imported. An import allowlist would report nothing at all about a domain module that simply called `fetch(url)`. The last is the loader-and-dependency sweep, which closed a category rather than a spelling: review found three separate ways to load something the scan cannot follow -- a computed specifier, `createRequire` from `node:module`, and the same builtin spelled `"module"` -- and closing each by name left the next open. Approving every bare specifier per layer, and refusing `eval` and `Function`, closes all of them at once including `node:vm` and `process.getBuiltinModule`, which nobody had named. It translates no source case because the Python source has no such category: `importlib` aside, a Python module reaches another by importing it.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: The POSIX-only-anchor sweep matches a `baseDir` property in an object literal. An anchor passed positionally -- `layerDocument(layer, origin, "/srv/catalog", data)` -- is not matched.
inherited_limitations.why: The source has the same hole and in the same place: it matches `keyword.arg != "base_dir"`, so a positional third argument to `layer_document` escapes it too. Carried over rather than widened, because widening it is a change to what the case asserts and belongs in the belt that needs it. What is added instead is the non-vacuity assertion the source lacks, which is what would catch the sweep silently matching nothing at all.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: The scan reads specifiers, not resolved semantics, so a module reached through a specifier built at runtime -- `import(someVariable)` -- cannot be named. It is NOT ignored: the port records such an edge as `<computed>` and fails closed, so `no module imports interlock` and the no-I/O cases both turn red on it.
inherited_limitations.why: The source has the identical blind spot for the identical reason -- `ast.Import` carries a name, not a computed value, so `importlib.import_module(name)` is invisible there -- but it resolves it the other way, by silently seeing nothing. Failing closed instead was raised at review of this belt and is the one place the port is deliberately stricter than the source: an unreadable edge makes every check below optional, since one variable would let the module graph say whatever its author wanted. Nothing under `src/` computes a specifier today, so the first thing that does has to say why. A no-substitution template -- ``import(`interlock`)`` -- is statically known and is read as the literal it is, rather than being dropped by a scan that only recognised quotes.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: The POSIX-only-anchor sweep reads the expression written at the `baseDir` property. An anchor reached through a name -- `const ROOT = "/srv/catalog";` then `baseDir: ROOT` -- is not resolved, so a POSIX-only literal behind one identifier escapes it.
inherited_limitations.why: The source has the identical hole: `_posix_only_literal` accepts an `ast.Constant`, or a `Path(...)` wrapping one, and returns None for an `ast.Name`. Following the name means resolving a binding in its scope, which is a type checker's job rather than a boundary check's, and the wrappers that ARE unwrapped here (parentheses, `as`, `satisfies`, a call's first argument) were widened past the source precisely because they need no scope analysis. Raised at review of this belt and left open deliberately: the case is a second line of defence behind `test/support.ts`'s `absolute()`, and the windows-latest cells are the first.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: The anchor sweep exempts a call whose callee is named `absolute`, matched by NAME rather than by binding. A test that declared its own `const absolute = (value: string) => value` and wrote `baseDir: absolute("/srv")` would pass.
inherited_limitations.why: Establishing that the callee is `test/support.ts`'s helper rather than a local of the same name is binding resolution, which is the same line this file already draws at `isShadowedOrDeclared` and for the same reason: a type checker's job, not a boundary check's. The exemption exists to stop the sweep reporting the one helper that makes an anchor portable, and shadowing it with a function that returns its argument unchanged is a way of writing a POSIX-only anchor that takes more effort than writing one. Raised at review of this belt and left open deliberately; the windows-latest cells remain the first line of defence.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: The loader sweep matches `.constructor` as a property access and as a bracketed element access. Destructured out -- `const { constructor: F } = () => {}; F('return import("interlock")')()` -- it is a `BindingElement` and matches neither, so the `Function` constructor is reached under a name the sweep never sees.
inherited_limitations.why: A member of the class the entry below names, found by the review round after the two expression spellings were closed, and left open with it rather than closed by a third spelling. Destructuring is a third syntax for the same read, and a fourth exists as soon as somebody writes one: the value can be reached through a parameter default, through a `for...of` over a pair, or from any function that returns it. That is the enumeration this file stopped running, and the boundary it drew instead is the sentence the entry below states -- an evasion has to be written deliberately, in a shape a reviewer sees, which this one is. Recorded rather than fixed so that the limitation is countable; detecting it properly means resolving a binding, which is the line `isShadowedOrDeclared` already draws.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: The global sweep suppresses the wrong half of an export alias. `export { local as fetch }` names an export `fetch` and reads no global at all, but `isShadowedOrDeclared` suppresses an `ExportSpecifier`'s `propertyName` -- `local` here -- and reports the `name`, so a pure-layer module exporting anything under a forbidden global's spelling fails the case.
inherited_limitations.why: A false positive rather than a hole, and the mirror of the one an earlier round fixed for imports: in `import { fetch as loadRecord }` the exported name is `propertyName`, and in `export { local as fetch }` it is `name`, so the two specifier kinds need opposite halves suppressed and currently share one branch. Nothing under `src/` exports such a name today, which is why the suite is green and why this is recorded rather than urgent. Left open because the fix changes which nodes the sweep reports, and a rule tightened this many times is exactly where the opposite error hides: it wants its own planted case, not a line added at the end of a belt.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: The POSIX-only-anchor sweep peels parentheses, `as`, `satisfies` and angle-bracket assertions, but not a non-null assertion. `baseDir: "/srv"!` is a `NonNullExpression` wrapping the literal, so the sweep reads no literal and the guard does not fire.
inherited_limitations.why: The same family as the wrappers already peeled -- an operator carrying the literal's runtime value under a different node kind -- and missed when that list was written. The consequence is precisely what the case exists to prevent: the anchor is absolute on POSIX and drive-relative on Windows, so the failure arrives from the windows-latest cells rather than from the guard. Left open with the two above because it is the same one-spelling-at-a-time shape and belongs with a planted case rather than at the end of a belt. No anchor in `test/` carries a `!` on a string literal today, which is also why nothing here has ever exercised it.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: The loader sweep refuses every route by which a module loads something without looking like it -- an unapproved bare specifier, a computed specifier, `eval`, `Function`, `require`, `module`, `globalThis`, `global`, `process` beyond its approved members, and `.constructor` -- but it is not a sandbox. A module determined to load interlock can still compute its way there, because JavaScript decides at runtime what this scan must decide by reading.
inherited_limitations.why: A property of the language rather than a gap in the check, and stated so that a green run is not read as more than it is. The source has the same limitation and less exposure to it: Python reaches a module by importing it or by `importlib`, and offers nothing like `Object.constructor`. What the sweep guarantees is that an evasion cannot look like ordinary code -- it has to be written deliberately, in a shape a reviewer sees. Four review rounds were spent finding members of this class (a computed specifier, `createRequire`, `eval`/`Function`, `.constructor`), which is what established that enumerating them ends only by saying where the enumeration stops.

Two things the source's case has no need of go with it: no file under `src/` was passed over unrecognised, and the walk descends into `src/cadenza/` -- the Python half, which is not part of this graph -- ignoring exactly the files the Python scan does read (`.py`, and the `.pyc` compiled from one) rather than skipping the directory. A `.pyi` stub is not among them: `tests/test_import_boundaries.py` walks `rglob("*.py")` and does not match one either, so ignoring it here would have reproduced the same hole one extension smaller. Skipping the directory was the one region of the tree that `tsconfig.json` type-checks and the Python walk does not read, so a TypeScript module placed there would have been seen by neither.
